reason: Leaf scars can be crescent-shaped, and the examples describe the scar itself.
Peduncles can be ciliate. The examples fit, though some could describe other parts.
Grass leaf-sheath auricles are often kidney-shaped, and the examples describe the auricle.
Glumes can be bristly or bear bristles. Some examples describe a bristle borne on the glume, so the data needs a check.
Veins (mapped to vascular bundle) can be ridged on one surface, and the examples fit.
Nectaries can have ciliate margins, and the examples fit.
'Undeveloped' leaves (rudimentary or suppressed) are a real condition. The examples say undeveloped, not absent.
Wrong reading: 'stinging' describes the hairs, not the lamina. PATO_0001727 (disposition) is a generic attribute and does not mean 'bearing stinging hairs'. A hair-type rule is needed.
Ovaries can be asymmetrical, and the examples fit.
Inflorescence branches can be unbranched, and the examples describe the branches.
A lamina can be short, and the examples fit.
Pseudobulbs can be crowded (densely arranged) on the rhizome.
A strap-shaped (ribbon-like) petiole is a real condition. Some examples ('appendice ligulé') describe an appendage and are wrong.
Short shoots (brachyblasts, spurs) can be robust, and the examples fit.

Cotyledons can be superposed or stacked (folded). 'margin superimposed' and 'superposés transversalement' may mean something else, such as flower parts. A rule would need the part to be cotyledons and the wording to be about overlap.

A spurred leaf base means the base bears a spur. It is not shaped like a spur, so the PATO shape is a misreading. A rule would need to map 'spurred' to a has-part spur annotation, or to a value term for 'spurred'.
Rhizophores can be glabrous, and the examples fit. One example, 'white waxy', is unrelated.
The examples describe the dehiscence slit or line as transverse, not the anther. The right bearer is the dehiscence line or slit. A transversely attached anther is a different feature, 'versatile'.
A floral disc can be large, and the examples fit.
Whole plants or herbs can be flexuous in habit. Stems may be the better bearer in some cases.
Lamina lobes can be scaly, with scales on the surface, as in ferns. The examples fit.
Veins can be dark. This is a colour reading (low brightness) and fits the examples.
Moss papillae can be tall. The bearer is the papilla (cell), and the examples fit.
Grass leaf collars can be glabrous, and the examples fit.
A receptacle can be thin. Some examples describe a cup, so the data needs a check.
Fern laminae can be fertile (bearing sporangia), and the examples fit.
A lamina can have parallel sides, and the examples fit.
A calyx can be saucer- or plate-shaped (patelliform), and the examples fit.
A tree crown has a width or spread, and the examples give a spread in metres.
A placenta can be falcate or subfalcate. This is a minor mismatch but acceptable.
Sporangia can be elliptic, and the examples fit.
A sporangium can be thick, and the examples fit.
Rhizoids can be conspicuous, and the examples fit.
A leaf sinus can be closed, with lobes overlapping, and the examples fit.
A mesocarp can be waxy (e.g. in palms), and the examples fit.
Glumes can be suppressed (aplastic), as in grasses, and the examples fit.

The examples are about the number of glands or translucent dots. A portion of secretory tissue is not clearly a gland or dot. A rule would need to map 'glands few' to a gland class or a count pattern.
Cataphylls and scale leaves can be thin, and the examples fit.
Locules can differ in size (unequal or reduced), and the examples fit. A value term would be more precise.
A stem base can be bulbous, and the examples fit.
Buds can be narrow, and the examples fit.
The examples are colours (pallid, dark, golden, green). 'Optical quality' is too general. Use colour terms or the colour rule instead.
'Attached to' is a relation and needs a target (substrate, twig, rock). A rule would need to record the substrate or treat it as a habit or habitat term instead.
Shoots (stems) can be winged, and the examples fit.
Antheridia can be present or absent in bryophytes, and the examples fit.
An orchid labellum can be saccate (sac-shaped), which is a concave 3-D shape. 'Saccate' is a closer fit, so a more specific term may be better.
Pinnae can be keeled, but the French examples describe a median ridge on the rachis, not on the pinna. A rule would need to check that the bearer is the pinna.
A receptacle can be sericeous, and the examples fit.
A moss operculum can be inclined or erect, but one example is about a Nepenthes pitcher lid, which is the wrong part. A rule would need the moss context and a more specific orientation term.
Elaters have a length, and the examples are measurements in µm.
'Cleistocarpic' means the capsule does not open (indehiscent). That is not the same as a closed shape. A rule would need to map 'cleistocarpic' to indehiscent or to a dehiscence term.
The examples describe the cilia (appendiculate), not the endostome. The right bearer is the endostome cilium. 'Shape' is also too generic for the value 'appendiculate'.
The examples give how many cells a region or border has. This is a count of cells, not an amount of one supra-alar cell. A rule would need the counted-parts pattern with the region as the bearer.
Awns can be serrate, and the examples fit.
The base of a moss capsule (neck, hypophysis) can be differentiated or not.
The base of a moss capsule can be inflated, and the examples fit.
Gemmae can be short. Some examples describe the stalk, so the data needs a check.
The examples say the cell walls are porose, so the bearer is the cell wall, not the cell. A rule would need to move the bearer to cell wall.
Cauline leaves have a width, and the examples give measurements.
Capsules can be campanulate (bell-shaped), and the examples fit.
